video_title: Parallelism: Why More Cores Don't Always Help
core_insight: Parallelism only helps when work can be decomposed into independent pieces where coordination cost is less than the gain from extra cores; the serial fraction limits speedup via Amdahl's law.

scenes.voice: Why does adding more machines sometimes not make things faster? The answer is parallelism, and its limits.
scenes.visual: Single craftsperson making one item vs assembly line with multiple stations. Text overlay: latency rises, throughput stalls.
scenes.on_screen_text: One thread = one thing at a time

scenes.voice: A single execution thread can only do one thing at a time. Demand grows, I/O takes time, users want low latency and high throughput. You can't make one core faster forever.
scenes.visual: Graph of request rate rising, latency climbing, CPU idle gaps during I/O.

scenes.voice: The obvious fix is to run work concurrently. Think assembly line versus one craftsperson. Parallelism means splitting work so independent pieces execute at the same time.
scenes.visual: Animation of assembly line with multiple stations processing different items in parallel.

scenes.voice: Parallelism needs two things: decomposition and independence. Break the problem into units that can run without each other. If they need immediate coordination, you pay a synchronization cost.
scenes.visual: Two boxes: Decomposition and Independence. Red warning on lock icon.

scenes.voice: At system level this looks like a load balancer sending independent requests to multiple workers. Workers run in parallel, but shared state creates a bottleneck.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    Client --> LB[Load Balancer]
    LB --> W1[Worker 1]
    LB --> W2[Worker 2]
    LB --> W3[Worker N]
    W1 --> DB[(Shared State)]
    W2 --> DB
    W3 --> DB

scenes.voice: This is Amdahl's law. Speedup is limited by the serial fraction. If 10% of work must stay serial, max speedup is about 10x no matter how many cores you add. Coordination overhead, locks, and contention can make parallel slower than serial.
scenes.visual: Bar chart showing serial fraction limiting speedup as cores increase.

scenes.voice: So only parallelize work that is independent enough that synchronization cost is less than parallel gain. Minimize the serial part first, partition data, and design for idempotency.
scenes.visual: Order processing pipeline with validate and fraud check running in parallel, then join before charge.

scenes.voice: Parallelism is a throughput strategy, not a latency guarantee. It trades coordination complexity for more concurrent work.

mental_model: Think assembly line: throughput is limited by the slowest station, not sum of times. Identify the serial fraction first, then decide if decomposition gives net gain after coordination cost.
final_takeaway: Parallelism helps only when work is independent and coordination cost is smaller than the gain; the serial fraction always limits speedup.
